title: clickhouse-ruler / operations
description: Is the ruler doing its job. For whoever operates it: missed iterations first, then failures, duration, staleness and delivery (spec 8.6).

panels.title: Missed iterations
panels.description: A group whose evaluation took longer than its interval. The single most important signal here, because alerts are then silently late (spec 8.2). Anything above zero for more than a few minutes wants either a cheaper query or a longer interval.

panels.title: Tick delay
panels.description: How long after its scheduled tick a group's evaluation actually started. A group woken on schedule still waits on the ruler-wide query concurrency cap or on its source's own, and that lateness never overruns an interval, so missed iterations above read healthy for the whole of it (spec 8.8). Read against the group's interval, drawn here beside it.

panels.title: Evaluation failures
panels.description: Evaluations that did not happen, per rule, counted one per cluster the rule failed against. The rate beside it counts the same unit, so the two divide into a share: a rule matching four clusters with one down reads a quarter. A broken annotation is not one of these and has its own panel on the alert rules dashboard.

panels.title: Evaluation duration
panels.description: How long a group takes, against the interval it is configured to run on. A duration approaching its interval is the missed iterations above, about to happen.

panels.title: Time since last evaluation
panels.description: How long ago each group last finished. A group that has stopped evaluating climbs here whether or not anything failed, which is the case no failure counter reports.

panels.title: Alerts sent and send failures
panels.description: Delivery to Alertmanager. A failure counts the batch once however many alerts it held, because it delivered none of them.

panels.title: Notification latency
panels.description: Time spent posting a batch Alertmanager accepted. A failed send is not in here: its duration is the retry policy giving up rather than anything Alertmanager did, so it would fire this panel for a delivery outage that send failures already reports. High here with failures at zero is Alertmanager accepting slowly; failures above zero is a delivery problem whatever this shows.

panels.title: Alertmanager answering
panels.description: Whether the address in --alertmanager answers its own readiness endpoint, probed every 30 seconds. Zero on a ruler that has delivered nothing is the typo'd host this panel exists for: the send counters have no series until something fires, so an expression over send failures cannot fire on a ruler that was never asked to deliver anything. Zero on a ruler that was delivering is Alertmanager being down or not ready, which the send failures beside it will show as well. The probe sends no alert and touches no alert state, and it is deliberately not part of /-/ready: one Alertmanager serves every replica, so a readiness term here would take a whole deployment unready at once (spec 8.1, 8.2).

panels.title: Query cost
panels.description: What rules are reading, from the driver's own callbacks rather than from system.query_log. The rate is the number that matters: the same query is cheap hourly and ruinous every fifteen seconds. An empty team is a rule whose author set no team label.

panels.title: Query memory and duration
panels.description: Peak memory one evaluation's query reached on the server, against the max_memory_usage cap the source sends, and how long the ruler waited for it. Duration climbing here is what becomes a missed iteration above.

panels.title: Query latency by source
panels.description: How long queries took against each cluster, which is the question asked first when alerts arrive late: a rule evaluates against every cluster its selector matches, so duration by rule alone cannot say which one is slow. One cluster above the rest is that cluster; all of them together is the rule's SQL or a table that grew. The second series adds the wait for a slot, which is what the rule actually waited (spec 8.8).

targets.expr: histogram_quantile(0.99, sum by (source, le) (rate(clickhouse_ruler_query_duration_seconds_bucket[$__rate_interval]))) + histogram_quantile(0.99, sum by (source, le) (rate(clickhouse_ruler_query_queue_wait_seconds_bucket[$__rate_interval])))

panels.title: Queue wait, by cap
panels.description: What queries waited for a slot, at both caps. Per source is the cluster's own max_concurrent_queries, and only sources that set one appear: a small steady wait is the limit doing its job, a growing one is a limit set too low or a cluster gone slow with the limit containing it. Per group is the ruler-wide --query-concurrency cap, and it is the term that reads as a late group with fast clusters, because a group's rules all fire on one tick and a group with more rules than slots queues against itself. Read against the cap in slots and the queries in flight against it, which is saturation without waiting for the histograms to fill (spec 8.8).

panels.title: Configuration reload
panels.description: Whether the running configuration is the configuration on disk. A refused reload is silent otherwise: the rules that are running are valid, nothing about them looks wrong, and the ruler is evaluating last week's files. Zero on the first series means the last SIGHUP was refused and the previous version is still running, which stays zero until a reload succeeds, so read the log for the reason and the findings printed with it. The second series is how long ago the running configuration was read, which answers the other question: a reload that never arrived looks the same as a reload that was never needed (spec 8.2).

panels.title: Sources failing the user contract
panels.description: Sources whose ClickHouse user no longer meets the contract the checks rely on, by source and check. This one is yours to fix, unlike the rules broken while running on the other dashboard: a grant that went away, a setting a constraint now blocks, a readonly flag flipped. Rebuilt at startup and on every reload, so a series that disappears is the grant coming back, and a series that stays means the checks depending on it are answering less than they look (spec 8.2, 6.7.3).

panels.title: Re-check pass
panels.description: Whether the pass that catches a renamed map key is still running, and what it costs. This is the one feed whose silence reads as good news: rule/attribute-key is raised only by sampling recent data, so a pass that stopped reports no findings and looks exactly like an estate where nothing was renamed. The first series is how long ago a pass finished, read against --recheck-interval: comfortably under it is healthy, a multiple of it means passes are being dropped. The second is what the last pass took, which is the term that grows with the rule file while the interval does not, so a pass approaching its interval is the warning before the first drop. Both are empty on a ruler started with --recheck-interval=0 (spec 8.2, 10.4).

panels.title: Clusters the re-check could not sample
panels.description: Clusters that would not answer the pass, by source. Yours to fix, and deliberately not a finding against a rule author: the ruler could not ask, so it learned nothing about the rules reading that cluster, and raising one would blame them for an outage. What it costs is that rule/attribute-key keeps its previous answer for that cluster rather than being re-asked, so a key renamed while this is non-zero goes unreported. The log line beside it carries the database's own reply (spec 10.4).

panels.title: Running configuration
panels.description: Always 1, one series per configuration version, and it is here for its labels. `revision` is a hash of the rule files and team policy files the ruler loaded, which is the only revision it can state: it fetches nothing, so nothing hands it a commit. Two series at once across a fleet is two rulers evaluating different rules, whatever either of them was told the commit was. `rules_root` is the resolved root the files were read from, which is the worktree under git-sync, so the commit rides along without the ruler claiming to know that is what it is (spec 8.2, 10.2).

panels.title: Build
panels.description: Always 1, one series per build, and it is here for its labels: which version, commit and Go version each replica is running. Two series at once is a rollout in progress or a rollout that only half landed, which is the reading that explains two rulers behaving differently from the same files. `dev` is a binary built outside a release (spec 8.2).
